newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Two Italian banks follow in rate cut move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Two Italian banks follow in rate cut move.

text.p: Two further large Italian banks cut their prime lending interest rates on Friday after pressure earlier this month for lower interests rates from Italian prime minister Romano Prodi.

Banca Commerciale Italiana said it was cutting its prime rate by 0.5 of a percentage point to 9.5 percent and its top rate one percentage point to 16 percent, while Banco Ambrosiano Veneto cut its prime rate by the same amount to 9.5 percent and its top rate by 1.25 percentage point to 16.5 percent.
Both said the new rates would take effect from December 23.

This followed a move late on Thursday by Italy's biggest bank Istituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino which said it was cutting its prime rate 0.5 of a percentage point to 9.5 percent and its top rate 1.5 percentage point to 16 percent from Monday.
The prime rate is the rate at which Italian banks lend to their best customers and the top rate is the ceiling rate at which they lend to clients.

Prime minister Prodi on December 5 had urged Italian banks to cut lending rates saying lower inflation was not enough to guarantee economic recovery. He was speaking on the day November Italian consumer price index (CPI) inflation fell to 2.6 percent from October's 3.0 percent, the lowest level since June 1969.
Prodi said there was a growing gulf between rates charged to banks' best clients and the top rates for similar operations.

The Bank of Italy has cut its discount rate twice this year in July and October, both times by 75 basis points, and many economists expected a further cut after preliminary December inflation data to be published on December 19 and 20.

Last week, Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi called for a cut in Italian interest rates saying he believed that conditions were right for a cut in interest rates and argued that the real rate of interest in Italy, or the interest rate related to inflation, was still too high.
